card.hook: Neptune has stood on the Long Market with his trident raised, looking like he's hailing a very large taxi. He's a dark bronze shape against pale, tall town-house fronts, and that makes him easy to photograph.
card.stand_here: Stand near Długi Targ, about 79 m from the fountain, and face south. Neptune is directly ahead of you, right in front of the Artus Court.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to catch the fountain with the buildings around it. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for a closer shot of Neptune and his trident. Skip 0.5x for the fountain itself, because it pushes him far into the distance from here.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the statue on one of the vertical lines, then tap the bronze figure and slide to darker if the sky is bright so he doesn't turn into a silhouette.
card.best_time: Early morning usually means fewer people in the square. In the evening, switch on night mode and rest your phone against a wall or post if the buildings are lit.
card.selfie_here: Head toward the Green Gate end of the Long Market, where you can still see the fountain. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep Neptune over your shoulder. This end of the square is a good place to frame him, but we haven't confirmed it as a selfie spot, so check your screen and adjust.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand toward the Green Gate end and keep the fountain, the Artus Court and the Main Town Hall tower in the shot, with the fountain slightly off-center.
card.challenge: Get Neptune on a gridline with the tall house fronts behind him, then add a few strangers walking by to show how big the square is.
card.good_to_know: The bronze figure was cast in 1615 and weighs 650 kilograms. The fountain didn't open until 9 October 1633, after delays that included a war and the designer's death. A year later it got a fence with gilded Polish Eagles, and it was fully renovated in 2011-2012.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Długi Targ, about 79 m from the fountain, and face south. Neptune is directly ahead of you, right in front of the Artus Court.

card.hook: St. Mary's Church is about 105 metres long, so from close up it simply won't fit in your photo. Don't fight it: walk to the cobbled street where the dark brick walls close off the end of the road and do the work for you.
card.stand_here: Stand on ulica Mariacka, about 54 metres east of the church, so the church is to the west of you. Face west, looking back up the street, and the church closes off the end with the house fronts and porches framing each side.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the street and the church together. Try 0.5x if you want more of the house fronts and the tower, or 2x (or higher, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the church at the end of the street.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the street down the middle with the church in the centre, and hold the phone level so the tower doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Wait a moment for people to pass, or let a few walk through on purpose to show how big the street is. If the church looks dark against a bright sky, tap the church and slide the picture a little brighter.
card.selfie_here: On the cobbles of Mariacka Street, face down the street toward the Motława so the church is behind you. Use the front camera (try 0.5x) and hold it a bit low so the brick tower fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand inside the Mariacka Gate (Brama Mariacka) and shoot back along the street while you stand in front of the church at the far end, so it fills the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The street is open public space, but the church is a place of worship. The tower terrace is a separate, ticketed visit, so check the official site for visiting rules before you go.
card.challenge: Find the exact spot where the church sits dead centre at the end of the street, then take one shot with nobody in it and one with a few strangers for scale. Which one wins?
card.good_to_know: St. Mary's was completed in 1502 in the Brick Gothic style and is counted among the largest brick churches in the world. Locals call it the Crown of Gdańsk. Building began on the present church in 1379, and the Baroque Royal Chapel next to it was finished in 1681.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on ulica Mariacka, about 54 metres east of the church, so the church is to the west of you. Face west, looking back up the street, and the church closes off the end with the house fronts and porches framing each side.

card.hook: A red tower leans over a rough wall of rubble, and no, your phone isn't tilted. It's meant to look like that, and it's one of Gdańsk's most striking modern buildings.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plac Władysława Bartoszewskiego, in front of the main entrance, and face the building. Follow the compass direction on the map for the last few steps.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the tower, the rubble wall and the plaza in one shot. Switch to 1x for a tidier view of the tower above the entrance. Try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the texture of the wall or the top of the tower.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the wall's edges up with the vertical lines, so only the tower looks like it's leaning.
card.best_time: Soft light early in the morning or late in the afternoon usually flatters the red tiles and the rough wall. Early also tends to mean fewer people in front of the entrance.
card.selfie_here: Go to the wide steps leading down from the square toward the entrance, with the angled red tower behind you. Use the front camera, switch to the wide view if your phone has one, and let the tower rise over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Stand by the Witold Pilecki statue outside the entrance, and ask a passer-by to photograph you from the plaza so the tower rises behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The square in front of the museum is an open public space.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the tower's lean looks totally deliberate, with the wall's edges perfectly straight and a slice of plaza at the bottom.
card.good_to_know: The museum was set up in 2008 and its exhibits opened to the public in 2017. The Gdynia-based Kwadrat studio designed the building, which covers roughly 23,000 square metres in three main spheres. The leaning tower is 40 metres tall, and a statue of Witold Pilecki was added in front of the museum in 2019.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Plac Władysława Bartoszewskiego, in front of the main entrance, and face the building. Follow the compass direction on the map for the last few steps.

selfie_spots.why: The angled red-clad tower is the building's most distinctive facade, and the square above it gives a clear view of it for a self-portrait.

card.hook: Picture a giant rust-red ship hull parked in the middle of Gdańsk, with a few tiny people strolling past its foot. That's the European Solidarity Centre, and it's built to look just like that.
card.stand_here: Walk to the phone icon on the map, which sits at the middle of the European Solidarity Centre's outline. Face the walls and take a step or two sideways until they stop leaning.
card.zoom: The building is about 158 m across, so use zoom 0.5x to get the whole front in. Switch to 1x for a calmer shot of one section, and try 2x (if your phone has it) for details like a window or the join between two walls.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line up one long edge of the wall with a horizontal line, so the building stands straight.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kinder to big walls than midday sun. On a cloudy day the surfaces look nice and even.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the cobbles in front of the blue gatehouse at Gate No. 2 of the Gdańsk Shipyard, under the STOCZNIA GDAŃSKA sign. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if you can, and hold the phone a little low so the centre's rust-red walls rise behind the gate over your shoulder. Or stand at the shallow pool below the steel piers of the entrance front, facing the glazed side entrance, so the entrance front fills the background.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the far side of the reflecting pool at the Monument to the Fallen Shipyard Workers of 1970, while you stand by the monument with the centre behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed for personal use, but check for restrictions on certain exhibits or areas. Check the official site before you go, in case access to parts of the building or grounds is limited.
card.challenge: Catch one person walking past the wall so the building looks as huge as it really is, then see if your friends guess it's a museum and not a ship.
card.good_to_know: The centre opened on 31 August 2014, the anniversary of the 1980 Gdańsk Agreement. FORT Architects won an international competition in 2007 to design it, and the walls are meant to recall the hulls of ships built at the Gdańsk Shipyard. Inside, there are around 2,000 exhibits and about 100,000 books and documents, so it's worth spending time there once you have your pictures.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to the phone icon on the map, which sits at the middle of the European Solidarity Centre's outline. Face the walls and take a step or two sideways until they stop leaning.

card.hook: Picture a street that decided to be a square: one long, open stretch with tall, narrow town houses standing shoulder to shoulder on both sides. Your eye gets pulled straight down it, which is exactly why it's so fun to photograph.
card.stand_here: Stand near Długi Targ, about 450 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to see how the view looks, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to bring the far end of the square closer. Save 0.5x for when you're walking in the square itself, where it helps fit the full height of the facades.
card.make_it_pop: Turn the gridlines on so the rooflines stay level, then tap the brightest part of the buildings and nudge it a little darker so the pale walls don't wash out.
card.best_time: Morning is likely your best bet, with the sun behind you lighting up the house fronts. It's also usually less crowded early, and summer middays can get busy.
card.selfie_here: Head to Neptune's Fountain on Długi Targ and stand at the fountain's front edge, opposite Artus Court. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone offers it, and the square's colourful facades will fill the frame behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand near the Green Gate at the east end of the square and shoot back into it, while you stand in the market with the full square behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Please don't climb on the fountain basin or touch the bronze figure. It's a historic monument, not a seat. The square is public, but if you plan to visit a museum or building around it, check the official site first.
card.challenge: Keep the phone upright for one shot of those tall facades, then turn it sideways for the long view down the street, and see which one you like better.
card.good_to_know: The market dates to about the 13th century, when it began as a merchant road. The Latin name Longa Platea first appears in 1331. For centuries Polish monarchs entered the city this way on ceremonial visits, and the wealthiest citizens lived along it, which helps explain the grand frontages.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Długi Targ, about 450 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west.

card.hook: Neptune's Fountain is the perfect photo bouncer: it stands right in front of Artus Court, so your picture already has a foreground before you do anything. Behind it, the tall, decorated façade is covered in statues of heroes.
card.stand_here: Stand in Długi Targ (the Long Market), in front of Artus Court with Neptune's Fountain between you and the building. Face north-west so the fountain sits in the foreground and the façade rises behind it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the fountain and façade together. If the square is packed and you can't step back, switch to 0.5x. Then try 2x or higher (depends on your phone) to pick out the statues and the gable.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the fountain on the lower third and let the façade fill the top, then tap the façade and drag the slider a little darker so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Late afternoon or evening gives you golden light and a lit-up façade. In the evening, try night mode and keep your phone steady against your body.
card.selfie_here: Stand at Neptune's Fountain on the Long Market with the Artus Court façade directly behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x so more of the building fits, and arrive early if you can, because one guide says that helps avoid tour groups.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back in the open square, across from or a few steps back from the fountain, while you pose at the fountain so the whole façade fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally permitted inside Artus Court without flash. If you plan to go inside, check the official site first.
card.challenge: Zoom in and find Fortuna on the gable, then see if you can get her in a shot without any tourists' heads in the way.
card.good_to_know: Artus Court was the merchants' meeting house where wealthy traders and visiting foreigners gathered in the evenings, and today it's a branch of the Gdańsk History Museum. The façade was rebuilt in 1617 by Abraham van den Blocke in Dutch Mannerism style. Inside, a Gothic hall holds an 11-metre tiled stove from the 1540s, and the building was badly damaged in 1945 and rebuilt after the war.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Długi Targ (the Long Market), in front of Artus Court with Neptune's Fountain between you and the building. Face north-west so the fountain sits in the foreground and the façade rises behind it.

card.hook: Mariacka Street is a tunnel made of tall, dark townhouses, with a big church waiting at the far end. Stand in the right spot and your phone does the composing for you.
card.stand_here: Stand inside Brama Mariacka, the gate at the Motława waterfront end, and face up the street toward St Mary's Basilica. The street runs west from the gate to the basilica, and it's about 2 minutes on foot to the middle of the street.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the gate's arch frames the street like a picture border. If the whole arch won't fit, tap 0.5x and keep your phone level. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) pulls the basilica closer to the houses.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the street or the church, then drag the slider to make it slightly darker so the sky at the end of the street doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Early morning is your best bet, when the cobbles are quiet and empty. Crowds build through the day. Blue hour or early morning also gives you a reflection from the waterfront.
card.selfie_here: Try standing under the arch of Brama Mariacka with the street and basilica behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the landmark over your shoulder. For a different backdrop, stand on the cobbles in front of the gabled houses with the gargoyle gutters.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across the Motława on the Long Waterfront, pointing their phone at Brama Mariacka, while you pose by the gate.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos on the street are fine, but many amber shops don't allow photos inside and put up signs saying so. Ask first if you want to shoot in a shop.
card.challenge: Get the arch making a neat border around the basilica, then walk up the street, turn round, and catch the reverse view with the houses leading back to the gate.
card.good_to_know: Mariacka Street is a narrow cobbled lane lined with tall, dark townhouses with gabled fronts and gargoyle terraces. St Mary's Basilica stands at the far end. It's a pedestrian street and open to everyone, so these views are free.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand inside Brama Mariacka, the gate at the Motława waterfront end, and face up the street toward St Mary's Basilica. The street runs west from the gate to the basilica, and it's about 2 minutes on foot to the middle of the street.

card.hook: Two chunky brick towers, one giant wooden arm stretched over the river: the Gdańsk Crane looks like it's about to lift a ship out of the Motława. It's easy to spot, even in a small phone frame.
card.stand_here: Stand near Nabrzeże Hanzy, about 60 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. The crane is straight ahead of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole crane with some river around it. Use 0.5x only if you have to stand close, and keep the towers straight. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the timber frame and the brick arch below it.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the two brick towers up with the vertical lines, with the crane slightly off-centre and some water in front.
card.best_time: Early morning or evening usually gives softer light and fewer people on the quay. After dusk, try night mode with your phone braced against a railing or wall. A visitor's tip says the crane is lit up at night.
card.selfie_here: Try the bridge over the Motlàwa on the side facing the Old Town, with the crane behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if you want more of the crane in, and hold your phone upright. A visitor's tip says the crane looks striking there under its night lights.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the Green Bridge (Zielony Most) to aim toward the crane from the right-hand side of the channel, with you and the full crane in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The crane now houses a museum, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.
card.challenge: Can you get the crane's wooden frame, a moored boat and a bit of river all in one shot?
card.good_to_know: The crane was finished by 1444 and was the largest port crane in medieval Europe. It was badly damaged in 1945 and rebuilt between 1956 and 1959. After a long renovation it reopened on 30 April 2024 and now houses a branch of the National Maritime Museum.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Nabrzeże Hanzy, about 60 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. The crane is straight ahead of you.

selfie_spots.detail: on the bridge across the Motława river, standing on the side facing the Old Town, with the crane behind you
selfie_spots.why: A visitor's tip says the crane is lit up at night, so this is the best time for photos, and a self-portrait with the crane behind you looks striking under those lights.

selfie_research.notes: Only one selfie spot was found. The TripAdvisor tip does not name the bridge, so check on a map which crossing is meant. The Green Bridge comes from a photography blog about reflection shots of the crane, and those photos show the crane alone, so the passer-by should deliberately include the visitor. Two sources (Airial, a TripAdvisor review) say nearby areas may be closed or under construction, which can limit shooting positions. No page mentions selfie sticks or tripods. Airial says personal photography is generally allowed inside the crane and museum, while professional shoots or drones may need permits; I left this out of rules because it is not a selfie-stick or tripod rule.

card.hook: Stand in the Long Market and the whole square seems to funnel your eye to one slim tower, with a fountain out front and colourful houses lining both sides. It's a ready-made postcard, and you barely have to try.
card.stand_here: Stand in Długi Targ, at the Neptune Fountain end of the square, and face the Main Town Hall. The tower closes the far end, with the fountain and the colourful tenement facades in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the classic view down the square. Try zoom 0.5x if you want the fountain and facades big in the foreground, and zoom 2x (if your phone has it) to pick out the tower and its weathervane.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the tower, then drag the slider to make the shot a touch darker so the sky keeps its colour and the facades don't wash out.
card.best_time: Go at sunrise, before the visitors and café seating arrive. After rain, ulica Długa gives you reflections on the wet paving.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside or in front of Neptune's Fountain on Długi Targ with the Town Hall behind you, so you get a colourful foreground and the tower right behind. Or walk toward the Green Gate end, face away from the Town Hall, and use the front camera (zoom 0.5x if your phone offers it) so the tower sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to take your photo on Chlebnicka Street, where the buildings frame the Town Hall tower (you may need to walk the street to find the framing).
card.rules_and_safety: On ulica Długa, wait until passing vehicles have gone before stepping out for a low shot. Inside the Town Hall, photos are allowed without flash.
card.challenge: Zoom in and catch the gilded king on top of the tower, then see if you can get him in a shot with the fountain too.
card.good_to_know: The oldest fragments of the Town Hall date from 1327 to 1336, and the tower went up between 1486 and 1488. After a fire in 1556 it was rebuilt with Renaissance touches by Dutch architects, and in 1561 a gilded figure of King Sigismund II Augustus was set on top as a weathervane. It was badly damaged in the Second World War, was largely rebuilt by 1952, and today it houses the city's history museum.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Długi Targ, at the Neptune Fountain end of the square, and face the Main Town Hall. The tower closes the far end, with the fountain and the colourful tenement facades in front of you.

card.hook: Count the gables on the Great Armoury and you'll get four, standing shoulder to shoulder like four separate houses. It's actually one building, and it's a bit of a show-off.
card.stand_here: Stand near Tkacka, at the phone icon on the map, about 55 m south of the subject. Face north and the whole front, with all four gables, fits in one view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole façade. If you can't fit all four gables in, switch to 0.5x. Then try 2x to 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out the carved reliefs high up.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the façade, then slide it a little darker if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Early morning usually means fewer people in your shot. Soft light in the morning or late afternoon, or a bright overcast day, helps the carvings show without harsh shadows.
card.selfie_here: Try the west end of Piwna Street, facing the façade, and go in the morning for the best light. Use the front camera at arm's length and keep the gables over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Targ Węglowy square in front of the building, where the main face can be seen, while you pose with the gables behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the façade from the square outside. For exhibitions or the interior, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Hunt for the carvings up high: can you spot Athena, the soldiers of Gdańsk and the exploding cannonballs?
card.good_to_know: The Great Armoury was built between 1600 and 1605 to a design by Anthonis van Obbergen, and it's described as the city's finest example of Mannerist architecture. It was an arsenal until 1793. After severe damage in 1945 it was rebuilt between 1947 and 1951, and today it houses the Academy of Fine Arts.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Tkacka, at the phone icon on the map, about 55 m south of the subject. Face north and the whole front, with all four gables, fits in one view.

selfie_spots.why: Sources describe this as the spot where the façade is lit well in the morning and glints under streetlights at night, making it a good backdrop for a close-up.

card.hook: Four statues stand along each side of the top of this gate. They're called things like Peace, Freedom, Justice and Prudence, and a Latin motto runs right across the front. It's a lot of gate, and it looks great on a phone.
card.stand_here: Walk to Targ Węglowy, the open square in front of the gate's western face. Face the gate and shoot it head-on, so you see the gilded statues and the Brotherhood of St. George building next door.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole gate. If the square is busy, or you want the Brotherhood of St. George building in the frame too, tap zoom 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the statues along the top.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the centre of the arch on the middle line and keep the phone upright so the arch and statues stay straight.
card.best_time: Come in the evening. The gate looks especially good at sunset, and even better once it's lit up at night. After dark, switch on night mode and tuck your elbows into your body to keep the shot sharp.
card.selfie_here: Try the western end of the Long Market (Długi Targ), just inside the Golden Gate. Face east down the square with the gate behind you, use the front camera and tap zoom 0.5x if your phone has it on the front. The gate should land over your shoulder, but check the frame before you smile.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Ulica Długa a short distance in front of the gate while you stand in front of the archway, so the whole gate fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The gate is a public arch you can walk through. The museum inside may be ticketed or have set hours, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get all four statues on one side of the gate in your frame, with the arch dead centre and nobody's head sticking in. Bonus points if you can find the Latin motto.
card.good_to_know: The gate was built in 1612-14 to replace a 13th-century Gothic gate. The architect was Abraham van den Blocke, and the style is Dutch Mannerism. The statues were designed in 1648 and rebuilt in 1878 after weathering damaged the originals. The gate was damaged by shelling in World War II but not destroyed, and it was repaired in 1957.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to Targ Węglowy, the open square in front of the gate's western face. Face the gate and shoot it head-on, so you see the gilded statues and the Brotherhood of St. George building next door.

card.hook: Brick arches, a busy skyline of little towers and the river sitting right next to them: the Green Gate is a lot of building to fit into one photo. The good news is it's perfectly symmetrical, so even a quick snap looks tidy.
card.stand_here: Head for the phone icon near Stągiewna, about 130 m east of the subject, and face west. From there the gate's whole front is in view.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to catch the whole gate and a bit of its surroundings. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the arches, windows and rooftop decoration. Use 0.5x only if people or railings get in the way and you need to step back, and keep the gate well away from the edges.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the gate's vertical edges with them so the towers don't lean.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or earlier in the day, when the light comes from behind you at the phone icon. A cloudy day works too, because the light is even and the brick colours still look good.
card.selfie_here: Try the middle of the green bridge over the Motława, with the gate in view across the water. Or try the Motława riverfront promenade (Ulica Długie Pobrzeże), opposite the gate. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the gate over your shoulder, and check the framing on screen before you smile, as the gate may sit a little off to one side.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Long Market (Długi Targ) at the gate end, facing the Green Gate, while you stand in front of the gate so it's behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay out of the roadway and out of other visitors' way while you line up the shot. The outside is fine to photograph from public space, but the building is a museum, so check the official site first if you want to go in.
card.challenge: Take three frames and pick the one with the fewest strangers' heads, then win bonus points for a clean shot of the central arch.
card.good_to_know: The Green Gate was built between 1568 and 1571 and shows clear Flemish influence. It was reportedly inspired by Antwerp City Hall. It was meant as a residence for Poland's monarchs, but the king never actually stayed here. Today it houses the National Museum in Gdańsk, and former President Lech Wałęsa's office is in one of its rooms.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the phone icon near Stągiewna, about 130 m east of the subject, and face west. From there the gate's whole front is in view.

card.hook: Here's a street that does half your job for you: tall, narrow house fronts line up on both sides and point your eye straight down the middle. Even a plain, straight-on snap looks like you planned it.
card.stand_here: Stand near Długa, about 85 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. Keep the street in the middle of your screen so the facades lead off into the distance.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view down the street. Switch to 0.5x if you want the full height of the facades, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for a doorway or carved house front.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the house fronts up with the vertical lines, then tap the brightest part of the buildings and slide it a little darker so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Early morning is usually quieter, and the softer light is kinder to the facades. Later in the day it's busier, which gives you more life but more people in your frame.
card.selfie_here: Try the Golden Gate (Złota Brama) at the street's western end: stand by the gate arch with the street running away behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and hold the phone upright so the buildings stay tall. Or head to Neptune's Fountain on Długi Targ at the eastern end for a classic backdrop.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the Golden Gate and shoot east up the street, while you stand further along the street so you're in the frame with the houses.
card.rules_and_safety: If you want to go inside any of the houses along the street, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Hold your phone upright, line up the house fronts with the gridlines, and let three strangers stroll into the frame. Bonus points if one of them looks like they're posing.
card.good_to_know: Long Street (Długa), also called the Long Lane, is part of the Royal Route and leads from the Golden Gate to the Długi Targ (Long Market) and the Green Gate. Along the way you'll pass named houses like Ferber House, Schumann House, Uphagen House and Lion Castle. It's one of Gdańsk's best-known sights, so expect company.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Długa, about 85 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. Keep the street in the middle of your screen so the facades lead off into the distance.

card.hook: This church looks like it's guarding a castle, not hosting a service. Plain red brick and a very tall roofline make it a great photo.
card.stand_here: Stand on ulica Lawendowa and face the basilica's side wall, with the houses along the street framing it on both sides. Step back to the far side of the street to fit more in.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get the whole church and the houses either side. Switch to 1x for a calmer, more natural look. Then try 2x to 5x, depending on your phone, for bricks, windows and roof details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and keep your phone level so the walls and house fronts stay straight.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light makes red brick glow. Go early if you want the street to yourself.
card.selfie_here: Head to Swantopolk II the Great Square, right beside the church, and pose next to the bronze statue of Duke Swantopolk II. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it a little low, then check what ends up behind you before you tap.
card.rules_and_safety: Scaffolding may still be on the Lawendowa side, so check when you arrive. If it's in the way, try Świętojańska and Szeroka for a clear view from the open square. The basilica is a working place of worship, so dress modestly and expect limits during services. If you go inside, keep your flash off.
card.challenge: Make the red brick wall run perfectly straight along your gridlines, with a house on each side like bookends.
card.good_to_know: St Nicholas's is a Brick Gothic church built between the 14th and 15th centuries, and the Dominican Order still runs it. It's the only historic church in central Gdańsk that came through the Second World War undamaged, so the inside still holds Gothic to Rococo furnishings. It closed in 2018 when cracks appeared in the vaulting, and repairs to the foundations and vaults were finished by 2022.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on ulica Lawendowa and face the basilica's side wall, with the houses along the street framing it on both sides. Step back to the far side of the street to fit more in.

selfie_spots.why: The bronze duke statue stands on this square right by the church, so it is the nearby feature a visitor can pose with.

card.hook: One of the stone faces on this old city prison lost its head in 1945, and finding the gap is a surprisingly fun little treasure hunt.
card.stand_here: Stand near Targ Węglowy, right where the phone icon sits on the map, and face the red-roofed building with its tall copper-topped tower.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to fit the long roofline and the tower in one go, or use 1x for a calmer, less stretched look. Then try 2x or 5x for the carved busts and the copper top.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the red roof, then slide the brightness a little darker so the sky stays blue and the roof keeps its colour.
card.best_time: A bright overcast day gives soft, even light that suits the red roof, and morning or late afternoon adds warmth. Check where the sun is first, because shooting straight into it turns the tower into a silhouette.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the Targ Węglowy (Coal Market) square with the Prison Tower behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x so the tower fills the frame over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from Długa Street facing west, so the Golden Gate is in front and the Prison Tower stands just behind it.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the outside from the surrounding streets. The building currently has no fixed public use, so check the official site before you go if you hope to get inside.
card.challenge: Zoom in on the busts and find the one that lost its head, then pose next to a whole one for the comparison.
card.good_to_know: The building went up beside the city walls in the 14th century and was rebuilt and enlarged by Anthonis van Obbergen between 1593 and 1604. It stayed the municipal prison until 1861, which is where its name comes from. An amber museum used it from 2006 until 2021.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Targ Węglowy, right where the phone icon sits on the map, and face the red-roofed building with its tall copper-topped tower.

Opening hours vary by source (one says the museum was closed until April, another says closed in winter), so check before visiting if you plan to enter the courtyard or tower.

card.hook: Picture a riverbank where, at one time, as many as 300 granaries stood shoulder to shoulder. Granary Island gives you water, old brick-and-timber warehouse shapes and the Main City skyline across the river, all in one shot.
card.stand_here: Stand near Pszenna, at the phone icon on the map, about 90 m south-west of the subject, and face north-east.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the river, the bridge and the granaries together. Go to 0.5x if you're close to the water and want the whole row of buildings. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for gables, brickwork and the Milk can Gate.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the sky, then slide the picture a little darker so the sky keeps its colour and the brick looks rich.
card.best_time: After dusk, switch on night mode to catch lit buildings reflected in the river, and rest your elbows on a rail to keep the phone steady. If the water is moving, try a Live Photo and pick the best frame.
card.selfie_here: Try the cobbled Ulica Stągiewna in the island's rebuilt core, which you reach by crossing the Green Bridge (Zielony Most). A travel blog lists it as a photo spot, so use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tuck the granary gables behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: On the Long Embankment (Długie Pobrzeże), near the rotating footbridge (Kładka Św. Ducha), ask a passer-by to face the island while you stand in front of them with the river and the island behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The island and its riverside are open public space, but buildings such as the museum may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find a spot where a gable or a bridge frames the scene, and get a bit of river in the foreground. Bonus points if you catch a reflection!
card.good_to_know: Granaries have stood on this bank since the 14th century. The island itself only appeared in 1576, when the New Motława was dug out. Much of the northern part was lost in March 1945 during the siege, so old and new buildings now sit side by side. The Milk can Gate (Brama Stągiewna), from 1517-1519, is another good subject.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Pszenna, at the phone icon on the map, about 90 m south-west of the subject, and face north-east.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a clear 'best selfie with the island behind' spot; both selfie entries are inferred from street or view descriptions and are lower confidence. The ask-someone spot rests on old Polish photo-archive captions and a photo gallery caption, not on a guide recommending a photo position. The AmberSky observation wheel is on the island, but its sources describe it as a ride with views, not a place to photograph from outside, so I left it out. No page stated selfie-stick or tripod rules, and none mentioned a safety point. Some sources are several years old.

card.hook: A red-and-black steamship parked in front of old brick granaries, with the Old Town skyline peeking out behind her. It's the kind of scene that makes your phone feel clever.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Ołowianka quayside directly in front of the SS Sołdek, on the Motława waterfront beside the granaries. Face the ship so the whole hull fits in your frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the full hull, the granaries and the river in one shot. If the quay is crowded or you can't step back far enough, try zoom 0.5x. Zoom 2x or more is good for details like the funnel, rigging or bow.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the red hull, then slide the brightness down a touch so the sky and water keep their colour and the dark paintwork doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, when the sun lights up the waterfront and the ship. Guides recommend it.
card.selfie_here: Try the Ołowianka quay beside the ship's stern, with the hull behind you. Use the front camera, switch to zoom 0.5x if you can, and hold the phone a bit lower so the ship fills the background.
card.ask_someone: If someone is on the Długie Pobrzeże embankment across the river, they can shoot the whole hull with you standing on the Ołowianka side.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is banned inside the 'Sołdek and its Times' exhibition, so keep the phone in your pocket there. Keep your phone and yourself away from the quay edge, and hold the handrails on steep stairways if you go aboard.
card.challenge: Line the waterline up with the lower gridline and leave a strip of water in front, so the Sołdek looks properly moored and not cropped.
card.good_to_know: The Sołdek was the first ship built in Gdańsk after the Second World War, and the first seagoing ship completed in Poland. She was the first of 29 Project B30 ships built at the Gdańsk Shipyard between 1949 and 1954. She's named after Stanisław Sołdek, one of the shipyard's shock workers, and she once played a Japanese steamer in the film Persona Non Grata.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Ołowianka quayside directly in front of the SS Sołdek, on the Motława waterfront beside the granaries. Face the ship so the whole hull fits in your frame.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a spot where a visitor takes a selfie with the Sołdek directly behind them, so the Ołowianka quay pick is an inference from waterfront photo locations. The Długie Pobrzeže ask-someone spot rests on a Polish photo caption ('view of the ship from Długie Pobrzeże street') and does not give the exact camera position. The museum's English page also has a 'Photography prohibited' heading, which appears to refer to a temporary exhibition, not the whole ship, so check on arrival. Selfie-stick rules were not stated on any page, so none are reported.
